title: Escalation: stable fallback and ramp-down controller for hosted 5xx/timeouts
creator: Sophie Kim
description:
Summary:
During recent customer escalations we observed simultaneous increases in 5xx and timeout rates driven by a combination of tenant retry amplification, long-lived streaming handoffs, and under-warmed dedicated pools. This ticket introduces a coordinated ‘ramp-down controller’ and a stable fallback fastpath to reduce customer-visible 5xxs while preserving correct idempotency semantics and minimizing manual intervention for escalations.

Goals:
- Rapidly halt retry amplification at the edge without global outage risk.
- Provide a per-tenant fastpath for escalated customers that bypasses non-essential middleware and routes to warmed capacity when available.
- Add an automated ramp-down controller that observes service-level signals (5xx rate, queue length, socket contention) and progressively reduces retry multipliers, admission burst sizes, and background warm-start behavior.
- Deliver an incident playbook to run alongside the automation with clear de-escalation and rollback thresholds.

Non-goals:
- Replace long-term fixes to KV cache serialization or kernel-level fixes — those are tracked separately.
- Permanent changes to default retry semantics for all customers. This is an incident mitigation path only.

Design notes and trade-offs:
- Edge retry suppression: prefer transient header-based signaling from the controller (x-rwz-escalation: suppress-retries) rather than changing client SDKs. This limits blast radius and allows SDKs to remain compatible.
- Fastpath selection: use existing tenant priority table + a short-lived session affinity token to route to warmed Dedicated pools when available; fall back to reduced-batch hosted variants if not. This adds complexity to routing policy but isolates escalated traffic.
- Ramp granularity: controller operates in four tiers (Normal -> Alert -> Contain -> Quiesce). Each tier applies incremental controls (reduce per-request retry multiplier, shrink admission windows, disable background prefetch). We favor small-step automation to avoid overreaction.
- Observability: new metrics required (ramp_tier, edge_retry_suppressed, fastpath_routes, warmed_pool_warmup_seconds). All must be visible in Console routes dashboard and incident runbook.

Implementation plan (phased):
1) Feature flags + header contract (3 days): implement header-based suppression at edge NGINX/LB layer; add feature flag to gate controller activation.
2) Fastpath routing shim (4 days): routing layer changes to consult escalation table and affinity token; minimal fallthrough rules.
3) Ramp-down controller (5 days): controller reads aggregated telemetry (per-region 5xx rate, queue length, socket contention), calculates tier, emits header flags and adjusts admission multipliers in the admission service.
4) Playbook + dashboards (2 days): document runbook, create SLO-based automated alerts, and a one-click rollback button in Console.
5) Canary + chaos test (2 days): synthetic tenant surge test with canary rollout (5% of edge nodes).

Testing & validation:
- Unit-level: controller logic, header emission, routing decisions.
- Integration: end-to-end through edge -> routing -> serving runtime with synthetic retries to ensure idempotency tokens preserved.
- Chaos: run a tenant surge test that reproduces retry amplification and validate that 5xxs drop and client-visible latency does not spike worse than baseline.
- Backwards compatibility: ensure SDK clients without special headers see no behavioral change until controller enabled.

Rollback and rollback metrics:
- Immediate rollback: flip feature flag to disable controller or remove header emission.
- Rollback indicators: if errors increase >10% above pre-change baseline within 15 minutes, auto-rollback. If customer-visible latency increases by >25% for escalated tenants, rollback.

Open questions / risks:
- Risk: routing to dedicated warm pools could starve other customers if warm pools are small. Mitigation: enforce per-tenant caps and circuit breakers on the dedicated pool router.
- Risk: header abuse by clients to request fastpath. Mitigation: require signed escalation token minted by Support/SEs and validate at the router.
- Observability gaps: need to ensure the Console sampling retention includes the new ramp metrics; otherwise debugging during incidents will be harder.

Artifacts and links:
- Design doc (Confluence): https://confluence.redwood.ai/hosted-stability/rampdown-controller
- Draft runbook (Drive): https://drive.redwood.ai/hosted-stability/rampdown-playbook-v1
- Initial routing shim PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/routing/pull/4812
- Controller PoC: https://github.com/redwood-inference/ops-controller/pull/198

Acceptance criteria:
- Controller can be enabled via feature flag and reduces edge retry multipliers in simulated amplifying scenarios by >=60% within 2 minutes of entering Alert tier.
- Fastpath routes escalate-customer traffic to warmed capacity with correct idempotency preservation in 90% of test cases.
- Console displays ramp_tier, suppressed_retries, and fastpath_route counts for the last 30 days.
- Playbook is reviewed and approved by Support, SRE, and Product.

2026-03-13 - Marco Ruiz: Opened PR for edge header handling (routing PR #4812). Starting work on the controller core. Planning canary for 2026-03-18.
2026-03-13 - Support Team Lead (Jamal Ortiz): Provided escalation token lifecycle requirements; tokens must auto-expire after 8 hours and be revocable.
Runbook draft link: https://drive.redwood.ai/hosted-stability/rampdown-playbook-v1 (feedback requested from SRE/Support/PM)
